title: Hermann Göring: How He Cheated the Hangman at Nuremberg
question: How do you think Göring got the poison?
summary: Hermann Göring, Hitler's Reichsmarschall and the highest-ranking soldier in Germany, was the leading defendant at the Nuremberg trials. Found guilty on all four counts, he asked to be shot as a soldier; the court refused and sentenced him to hang. On the night before the executions of 16 October 1946 he killed himself with a potassium cyanide capsule, although he was guarded around the clock. Ten others were hanged by Master Sergeant John C. Woods. How Göring got the poison is still debated: a hair cream jar, an American lieutenant he gave his gold watch, or a fountain pen smuggled in by a young guard.

cover.note: sentenced to hang, cyanide the night before (true)

sentences: On the night of 15 October 1946, guards in Nuremberg prison peered into the cell of Hermann Göring.
The man who had once been second only to Hitler was twisting in convulsions.
A doctor was quickly summoned, but Göring was dead within five minutes.
In a few hours, he was due to be hanged.
He was guarded around the clock, and yet he had a potassium cyanide capsule.
This is the story of the trial of the century, of the ten men who did hang, and of the poison nobody can fully explain.

chapters.title: The Second Man of the Reich
sentences: Hermann Göring had been one of the most powerful figures in the Nazi Party.
Born in Rosenheim, in Bavaria, he had been a fighter ace in the First World War, and the last commander of the wing once led by Manfred von Richthofen.
Wounded in Hitler's failed Beer Hall Putsch in 1923, he developed an addiction to morphine while receiving treatment.
He was Supreme Commander of the Air Force, the Luftwaffe, a position he held until the final days of the regime.
In 1940, Hitler promoted him to Reichsmarschall, a specially created rank, and he became the highest-ranking soldier in Germany.
By 1941, he was at the peak of his power and influence.
But his standing declined when the Luftwaffe proved incapable of preventing the Allied bombing of Germany's cities.
He increasingly withdrew from military affairs, to collect property and artwork, much of it stolen from Jewish victims of the Holocaust.
In April 1945, he sent Hitler a telegram asking to take over the leadership of the Reich.
In his last will and testament, Hitler expelled Göring from the party, and rescinded the decree that made him his successor.

chapters.title: The Trial of the Century
sentences: After the war, Göring was flown to a prisoner-of-war camp in the Palace Hotel at Mondorf-les-Bains, in Luxembourg.
There he was weaned off a mild morphine derivative, put on a strict diet, and lost 60 pounds.
His IQ was tested while he was in custody, and found to be 138.
In mid-1945, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States agreed to convene a joint tribunal in Nuremberg.
For the first time, individuals, not states, would be held responsible for breaches of international law.
By early 1946, there were a thousand employees from the four delegations in Nuremberg, about two thirds of them from the United States.
Each of the four powers appointed a prosecution team and two judges.
Of the 24 men indicted, Martin Bormann was tried in absentia, Gustav Krupp was too ill to stand trial, and Robert Ley had died by suicide.
On 20 November 1945, the trial began in the Palace of Justice, and all the defendants pleaded not guilty.
The next day, the American chief prosecutor, Robert H. Jackson, gave the opening speech.
When asked for his plea, Göring tried to read a lengthy statement, but the presiding judge, Sir Geoffrey Lawrence, told him simply to plead guilty or not guilty.
He was the second highest-ranking official on trial, behind the former admiral Karl Dönitz.
The charges against Göring included the plundering and removal to Germany of works of art and other property.
Göring then declared himself, in the sense of the indictment, not guilty.
He described the fact that the defeated Nazis received a trial as one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason.
It was the first use of simultaneous interpretation, and every defendant followed the trial through headphones.
Göring sat in the front row of the dock.

chapters.title: Göring in the Dock
sentences: The trial lasted 218 days.
Forced to remain silent in the dock, Göring communicated his opinions using gestures, shaking his head, or laughing.
He constantly took notes, whispered with the other defendants, and tried to control the erratic behaviour of Rudolf Hess, who was seated beside him.
During breaks, he tried to dominate the other defendants.
The defendants tried to blame their crimes on Hitler, who was mentioned 12,000 times during the trial.
On 29 November, the prosecution screened a film compiled from footage of the liberation of the Nazi concentration camps.
The film shocked both the defendants and the judges, who adjourned the trial.
In all, 249 journalists were accredited to cover the trial.
They also blamed other absent and dead men, including Himmler, Heydrich, Eichmann and Bormann.
Göring's own defence, the first to be presented, lasted from 8 to 22 March 1946.
On 31 August, closing arguments were presented.

chapters.title: The Verdict
sentences: The sentences were read on 30 September 1946.
Göring was found guilty on all four counts, and sentenced to death by hanging.
Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, Bormann among them.
In fact, Bormann had died on 2 May 1945, trying to escape from Berlin.
Seven, including Hess and Albert Speer, were sent to Spandau Prison to serve their sentences.
Three were acquitted.
Göring made an appeal, asking to be shot as a soldier instead of hanged as a common criminal.
The court refused.
The ten men who were hanged went to the gallows in the early morning of 16 October, a little more than two weeks later.

chapters.title: The Last Night
sentences: Göring asked for Lutheran last rites, but that was refused.
The executions were set for the early morning of 16 October.
The night before he was to be hanged, Göring committed suicide with a potassium cyanide capsule.
His death was slow and painful.
As the guards peered into his cell shortly before the execution, they saw him twisting in convulsions.
A doctor was quickly summoned, but Göring was dead within five minutes.
In his suicide note, he claimed to have possessed the capsule since he was imprisoned.
Since he was guarded around the clock, it was not clear how he had obtained the poison.

chapters.title: Ten Ropes
sentences: For their last meal, the condemned men were served sausage and cold cuts, potato salad and black bread, with tea to drink.
Starting at about 1:10 in the morning, the ten condemned men were led one at a time to the execution chamber.
The first was the former foreign minister, Joachim von Ribbentrop, followed by Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel.
The death sentences were carried out by the United States Army.
Three temporary gallows had been built in the gymnasium of Nuremberg Prison.
The executioners were Master Sergeant John C. Woods and his assistant, military policeman Joseph Malta.
Woods used the standard drop method, and some of the men did not die quickly, but strangled slowly.
Joseph Kingsbury-Smith of the International News Service wrote an eyewitness account of the hangings.
The Army denied claims that the drop had been too short.
The bodies were cremated in Munich, and their ashes scattered over the river Isar.

chapters.title: The Hangman
sentences: John Clarence Woods was born in Wichita, Kansas.
When the Army looked for a volunteer hangman in 1944, he falsely claimed previous experience in Texas and Oklahoma.
There is no evidence that the Army made any attempt to verify it.
Both states had switched to the electric chair long before.
Woods hanged 34 American soldiers in France, and Army reports suggest he took part in at least 11 bungled hangings.
After Nuremberg, he told reporters that he had hanged those ten Nazis, and that he was proud of it.
Time magazine credited him with 347 executions in a 15-year career.
He died just four years after Nuremberg, in 1950.

chapters.title: The Poison
sentences: To this day, nobody knows for certain how Göring got the poison.
At the time, speculation centred on a jar of his hair cream, where another cyanide capsule was later found.
Decades later, another theory focused on a US Army lieutenant, Jack G. Wheelis, who had been stationed at the trials.
Göring had given Wheelis his gold watch, his pen and his cigarette case.
Wheelis had since died, and it was theorised that he had retrieved the capsules for Göring.
Then, in 2005, a former US Army private, Herbert Lee Stivers, came forward.
He said he had given Göring medicine hidden inside a fountain pen, which a young German woman named Mona had asked him to smuggle into the prison.
He said he decided to speak out 60 years later, after his daughter convinced him.
He said he did not know what was in it until after Göring's suicide.
The prison psychiatrist, Douglas Kelley, called Göring's suicide an admirably defiant act against the prison authorities.
The man who had asked to be shot as a soldier had chosen his own death, a few hours before the rope.
So how do you think Göring got the poison? Tell me what you think in the comments.
